:::{#thm-inference-rules}
#### Common rules of inference

For [propositions](#def-proposition) $P$ and $Q$,
each of the following is a [rule of inference](#def-rule-of-inference):

1. modus ponens:
   $$
   \frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad P}{Q}
   $$
2. modus tollens:
   $$
   \frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad \neg Q}{\neg P}
   $$
3. disjunctive syllogism:
   $$
   \frac{P \lor Q, \quad \neg P}{Q}
   $$
4. simplification:
   $$
   \frac{P \land Q}{P}
   $$
5. conjunction:
   $$
   \frac{P, \quad Q}{P \land Q}
   $$
6. addition:
   $$
   \frac{P}{P \lor Q}
   $$

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

::: proof

For each rule, suppose every [premise](#def-logical-argument) is true, and show that the [conclusion](#def-logical-argument) is true.

1. By the definition of [implies](#def-implies),
   $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false.
   Here $P$ is true and $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true, so $Q$ is not false.
2. $\neg Q$ is true, so by the definition of [not](#def-not), $Q$ is false.
   If $P$ were true, $P \Rightarrow Q$ would be false,
   so $P$ is false and $\neg P$ is true.
3. $\neg P$ is true, so $P$ is false.
   By the definition of [or](#def-or),
   $P \lor Q$ is true only if $P$ or $Q$ is true,
   so $Q$ is true.
4. By the definition of [and](#def-and),
   $P \land Q$ is true only if both $P$ and $Q$ are true,
   so $P$ is true.
5. $P$ and $Q$ are both true, so by the definition of [and](#def-and), $P \land Q$ is true.
6. $P$ is true, so by the definition of [or](#def-or), $P \lor Q$ is true.

:::

:::
